name: The Assumption Lab
description: Revisit the fundamentals through liquidity, opportunity cost, compounding, and uncertainty.
tone: The model is confident. Ask it why.

topics.title: Separate flows, stocks, and constraints.
topics.text: Income and spending are flows over time. Net worth is a stock of assets minus liabilities. Neither alone measures liquidity: a valuable asset may not meet tomorrow’s bill without cost or delay. Start a financial decision with cash needs, obligations, time horizon, and uncertainty, not an isolated return.
topics.aside: This fictional household has $6,000 monthly take-home cash and $4,200 in essential outflows. Its net worth and job stability are deliberately unspecified.
topics.joke: Your house has equity. The grocery checkout prefers something more portable.
topics.prompt: Inspect the cash flow. Notice what the illustration cannot tell you.
topics.term: A STRONG BALANCE SHEET CAN STILL HAVE A TIMING PROBLEM
topics.everyday: A household with substantial home equity and volatile self-employment income may face a near-term liquidity gap. Conversely, a modest balance sheet can support a stable plan if liabilities and cash availability are well aligned. Separate realized cash income from paper gains, restricted assets, and new borrowing. Taxes and benefit deductions matter to spendable cash. A useful model identifies which obligations are certain, which resources are contingent, and which dates cannot move.
topics.connection: Before optimizing a return, specify the cash flow, stock of wealth, and binding constraint.
words: An amount measured over a period, such as monthly income.
An amount at a point in time, such as net worth.
The ability to meet cash demands without unacceptable delay or cost.
topics.assumptions: All money amounts and timing are invented for teaching. This is not a survey of prices, income, or tax rates. The flow view is a single example, not a recommended allocation.

topics.title: Allocate marginal dollars deliberately.
topics.text: A budget is a resource-allocation model, not a moral ranking of purchases. The opportunity cost of a choice is the next-best alternative forgone. Fixed costs, taxes, care obligations, and volatile income constrain feasible choices. A monthly surplus is not automatically an investable surplus if near-term liabilities are omitted.
topics.aside: After modeled essentials, $1,800 remains. Move flexible spending and observe the time to a $12,000 goal. No growth, income volatility, or taxes are added.
topics.joke: “All else equal” has once again failed to attend the meeting.
topics.prompt: Explore the allocation, then ask which missing fact would matter.
topics.term: OPTIMIZE WITHIN CONSTRAINTS; AUDIT THE CONSTRAINTS
topics.everyday: A spending plan can be evaluated by feasibility, resilience, and alignment with stated goals. Marginal spending choices should be compared with their next-best alternatives, while distinguishing fixed commitments from reversible decisions. A hypothetical percentage allocation says little without household context. Stress tests can expose a plan that works only under full employment, a single price path, or an assumed ability to defer bills. Positive surplus should be reconciled with irregular liabilities.
topics.connection: Opportunity cost connects consumption, debt repayment, reserves, and investing in the same framework.
words: The use of the next available dollar or unit of resources.
The next-best alternative forgone by a choice.
Whether a plan can satisfy its actual constraints.
An obligation that does not arrive on a regular monthly schedule.
topics.assumptions: Essentials are fixed in this illustration. Flexible spending and saving divide the remaining money. Goal periods = ceiling(goal ÷ saving per period). No interest, price changes, or income changes are modeled.

topics.title: Liquidity is an option with a cost.
topics.text: Accessible reserves can reduce forced borrowing or asset sales. Their opportunity cost depends on alternatives, but so does their value under a shock. Insurance can transfer specified losses; it leaves deductibles, exclusions, and counterparty or coverage considerations. Evaluate resilience across income, assets, obligations, and available support.
topics.aside: Start with $1,000 and add a monthly contribution for six months. Test a $2,500 shock. This stress case has no assigned probability and excludes insurance recoveries.
topics.joke: An illiquid asset is excellent at saying, “I’m worth a lot, technically.”
topics.prompt: Change contributions. Observe the uncovered cost, not just the balance.
topics.term: STRESS A PLAN AGAINST AN OBLIGATION
topics.everyday: A reserve held in accessible cash may earn less than a risky asset while still improving the household plan. It can preserve choice during job loss or a market decline. Correlated shocks matter: income and asset values can deteriorate together. Insurance coverage is contractual, not a general promise to restore every loss. Identify deductibles, exclusions, limits, and the timing of reimbursement before treating coverage as immediately available cash.
topics.connection: A resilience model asks whether the obligation can be met under stress, not only whether average wealth rises.
words: The value associated with being able to access money promptly.
Shifting specified losses under an agreement, such as insurance.
An examination of a plan under a defined adverse scenario.
topics.assumptions: Savings = starting cash + contribution × periods. A surprise is subtracted once when switched on. Savings cannot go below zero; the remaining cost is shown separately. No interest, investment returns, insurance payment, or new borrowing is included.

topics.title: Debt repayment changes the opportunity set.
topics.text: Interest avoided by repaying contractual debt is more predictable than a risky investment return, but liquidity, taxes, penalties, and flexibility can alter the comparison. APR alone may not capture every product cost. Model repayment using actual terms, and examine what happens if income falls before optimizing an expected return.
topics.aside: The example uses $10,000 at 9% APR with fixed monthly repayments. Interest is APR ÷ 12 on the opening monthly balance, then payment. Taxes, fees, and new borrowing are excluded.
topics.joke: The expected return has a beautiful résumé. The debt payment has a due date.
topics.prompt: Compare payment speeds without treating this model as a recommendation.
topics.everyday: A contractual borrowing rate and a probabilistic investment return are not interchangeable inputs. A comparison may also depend on deductibility, prepayment terms, rate resets, and the value of keeping access to cash. Those features are excluded here, so the model isolates repayment arithmetic. If payments do not cover interest, the starting balance does not decline. For variable-rate or daily-interest products, use the actual contract and payment dates rather than this monthly approximation.
topics.connection: Debt repayment, liquidity, and investment risk should be compared on a consistent after-cost basis.
words: The reduction of a debt through scheduled payments.
An annualized percentage measure of borrowing cost; product conventions differ.
A situation in which unpaid interest can increase the debt balance.
topics.assumptions: Interest = opening balance × APR ÷ 12, then the fixed payment is applied. The last payment may be smaller. No new charges, fees, daily calculation, payment timing variation, or tax effects. The comparison payment is a fictional fixed amount, not a real issuer’s minimum-payment schedule.

topics.title: Audit nominal growth, fees, and inflation.
topics.text: Compounding amplifies both growth and ongoing costs. Nominal returns describe account dollars; inflation-adjusted values describe purchasing power. Diversification can reduce concentration risk but cannot remove market loss. A smooth expected path is not a distribution of outcomes, and a positive expectation does not guarantee meeting a liability.
topics.aside: Compare a selected annual fee with a hypothetical 0.1% fee, holding everything else equal. Returns, fees, and inflation are constant assumptions. Values are before tax.
topics.joke: Decimals: tiny on the fee sheet, surprisingly ambitious over twenty years.
topics.prompt: Move fees and inflation. Then stress the ending value with a 20% fall.
topics.term: THE OUTPUT IS ONLY AS USEFUL AS THE ASSUMPTIONS
topics.everyday: At a fixed gross return, a larger ongoing fee leaves less money compounding. Inflation then translates nominal dollars into purchasing-power terms; taxes would require another layer. These are sensitivity calculations, not an investment forecast. For example, an invented one-period investment with an 80% chance of gaining 15% and a 20% chance of losing 40% has a 4% expected return. It still has a 20% chance of losing 40%. A positive average does not secure a bill due at the end of that period.
topics.connection: Judge a model by the decision it supports, the downside it exposes, and the assumptions it leaves outside the frame.
words: A value expressed in account dollars without an inflation adjustment.
What the money can buy after accounting for prices.
A probability-weighted average across modeled possible returns.
Changing assumptions to see how the output responds.
topics.assumptions: Nominal ending value = principal × (1 + (gross return − annual fee)/100)^years. Purchasing power divides that value by (1 + inflation/100)^years. Subtracting the fee from annual return is a simplified convention. The optional 20% drop is applied once at the end, to both comparison paths. No taxes, contributions, or changing returns. These are scenarios, not promised outcomes.

recap: Separate cash flow, net worth, and liquidity.
Evaluate resilience before chasing an optimum.
Compare fees, purchasing power, and downside risk.
action: Name an assumption that could reverse a decision.
Check a plan against a shorter deadline.
Compare costs using actual product terms.
artAlt: An analysis screen with two growth paths and a magnifying glass questioning the assumptions.
